mechanism: When recent volatility is high, daily exchange-rate moves exhibit volatility clustering, so future short-horizon changes should resemble previous high-volatility episodes.
When recent slope magnitude is high, the exchange rate is in a strong directional trend that is likely to persist for the forecast horizon.
When recent slope magnitude is low, the exchange rate is range-bound and mean-reverting, so low-trend historical segments are more informative.
When recent autocorrelation is high, successive daily changes are persistent and therefore high-autocorrelation historical segments are more predictive.
When recent autocorrelation is low, the daily exchange rate is choppy and mean-reverting, so low-autocorrelation historical segments are more predictive.
When recent daily difference magnitude is high, large jumps signal an information shock and similar jump episodes are more predictive of near-term volatility.
On working days, active trading and fixing flows dominate daily exchange-rate dynamics, making historical working-day segments more predictive than non-working days.
In winter, year-end rebalancing and holiday-thinned liquidity create distinctive daily exchange-rate patterns, so historical winter segments are more predictive.
Short-horizon exchange-rate volatility and liquidity follow a persistent hour-of-day cycle, so the current mid-day trading regime is best informed by same-hour historical sessions.
The current recent_level summarizes the accumulated net move in the exchange-rate state, so similar historical level environments are more informative for near-term continuation behavior.
Low recent volatility states tend to persist in FX because quiet risk appetite and range-bound order flow are sticky, making low-volatility history the most relevant comparison set.
When recent daily difference magnitude is low, the exchange rate is in a quiet news environment, and similar calm historical episodes better capture the stable short-horizon risk profile.

When recent slope magnitude is low, the exchange rate is range-bound and mean-reverting dynamics are more likely to persist than a sudden breakout, so low-slope history is the relevant comparison set.
When recent_autocorrelation is low, short-horizon exchange-rate moves are choppy, and retrieving low-autocorrelation windows with a short lag emphasizes the immediate reversal pattern.
Summer FX trading has reduced liquidity and seasonal participation, so same-season historical segments are more representative of the current summer trading regime.

Short-horizon FX dynamics differ between working and non-working calendar sessions because institutional order flow and market-making are materially thinner on non-working days, making same-session liquidity history more relevant.

High recent_slope_magnitude signals a directional macro impulse and trend regime where momentum and trend persistence are more likely than immediate mean reversion; similar high-slope histories capture the continuation profile.
